title: The Tai Shang Tractate of Actions and Their Retributions
attributionNote: The tract is presented as the instruction of Tai Shang, the Most High Lord Lao, and was widely circulated as a revelation. Its actual composition is anonymous, usually placed in the Song dynasty, and it became the model for the later morality books.
description: The Tai Shang Tractate is the most influential of the Chinese morality books: a short scripture on the working of retribution, in which the Most High Lord Lao teaches that good and evil deeds are answered, that the spirits of the household and the heavens keep account, and that the good are rewarded with long life, honour and peace while the wicked are visited with misfortune. It became a school text for ethical instruction and the parent of a whole genre of moral tracts.
historicalContext: The Kan Ying P'ien circulated widely in the Song and later, was commented on by Confucian and Buddhist as well as Daoist writers, and was printed in enormous editions for moral instruction. Legge printed a translation at the end of the second volume of his Texts of Taoism (1891), with a note on the tractate's character and its place in Chinese religion.
availabilityNote: Complete. Legge's translation of the tractate is streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time; it is a single printed text, presented here as one chapter with its paragraphs indexed. The volume's introduction and the appendixes that follow are not part of the work.
